design_detail: Prospective, non-randomized, unblinded drug-challenge study in the cardiac catheterization laboratory of Parkland Memorial Hospital / University of Texas Southwestern. 15 patients undergoing catheterization to evaluate chest pain were measured at three time points: at baseline, 15 minutes after intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg, and 5 minutes after an intravenous infusion of either saline (group I, n = 6) or labetalol 0.25 mg/kg over 2 minutes (group II, n = 9). Measures at each point: heart rate, mean arterial pressure and coronary arterial area by computer-assisted quantitative angiography of a proximal, a middle and a distal segment of the left anterior descending artery chosen as free of atherosclerotic narrowing. Allocation to saline or labetalol is not described as randomized and no blinding of patients, operators or image analysts is reported, so the parallel arms are a non-randomized comparison of an intervention and the within-person before-after change is the study's main evidence. Same group and same laboratory as the propranolol study (Lange et al., 1990), with the same intranasal cocaine dose; none of the patients had used cocaine before.
can_establish: That in 9 cocaine-naive catheterization patients, intravenous labetalol 0.25 mg/kg given 5 minutes earlier left the coronary arterial narrowing produced by intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg essentially unchanged (3.47 to 3.37 mm2, still below the pre-cocaine 3.80 mm2) while mean arterial pressure fell from 117 to 110 mm Hg; and that in 6 patients given saline instead, nothing changed after the infusion.
cannot_establish: Whether labetalol helps or harms people who present to hospital after using cocaine: no clinical outcome was measured, the patients had never used cocaine, and only one dose was given. It also cannot establish that labetalol is worse or better than propranolol (the two drugs were studied in separate papers with different control arms and no head-to-head comparison), that the degree of alpha- or beta-blockade achieved was adequate (none was measured, and heart rate did not fall), or that the labetalol and saline arms were comparable, since allocation was not randomized and the two arms differed at baseline.

sample.recruitment: Patients undergoing cardiac catheterization for the evaluation of chest pain at the same centre as the 1990 propranolol study; how they were approached or how many were eligible or declined is not reported (p. 608).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Undergoing catheterization for chest pain; none admitted to previous cocaine use; the paper states that no patient received beta-adrenergic blockers for more than 6 months before the study (the wording is ambiguous, see reporting issues), that all anti-anginal agents were stopped more than 12 hours before, and that patients were studied fasting after 5 to 10 mg of oral diazepam (p. 608). No exclusion criteria such as hypertension or recent infarction are stated, unlike the 1990 study.
sample.demographics: 7 men and 8 women, aged 40 to 79 years. 6 had angiographically normal coronary arteries and 9 had atherosclerotic disease (70% or greater luminal diameter narrowing of a major epicardial vessel: one-vessel in 5, two-vessel in 2, three-vessel in 2). Age, sex and disease distribution by arm are not reported (pp. 608-609).
sample.attrition: No patient is reported lost. 40 coronary arterial segments were analysed where the stated method (a proximal, a middle and a distal segment in each of 15 patients) implies 45; the 5 unanalysed segments are not accounted for (p. 608 methods against the abstract, p. 608).
sample.selection_effects: Middle-aged and older cardiac patients under investigation for chest pain, none of whom had used cocaine, given one controlled intranasal dose. Half the sample had obstructive coronary disease. The 6:9 split between saline and labetalol is unexplained and the arms differ at baseline (heart rate 83 against 71 beats/min, mean arterial pressure 96 against 107 mm Hg, coronary arterial area 4.59 against 3.80 mm2), so arm membership is not independent of the measured variables.

exposure.measurement: Both drugs given in the laboratory. Serum cocaine concentration measured from a blood sample drawn 15 minutes after the intranasal dose: 0.14 +/- 0.05 mg/L in the saline arm and 0.19 +/- 0.11 mg/L in the labetalol arm (Table I, p. 609). Labetalol concentrations were not measured and no index of achieved alpha- or beta-blockade is reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only. Single intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg, described by the authors as one half to two thirds the amount used for intranasal anesthesia and chosen for its established safety; then a single intravenous infusion of labetalol 0.25 mg/kg over 2 minutes, which the authors identify as the recommended dose and route for severe hypertension, or an equivalent saline infusion (pp. 608-610).
exposure.polysubstance: All patients received 5 to 10 mg of oral diazepam as premedication and iodinated contrast for angiography; anti-anginal drugs were withdrawn more than 12 hours earlier. No other drug or alcohol use is reported and no toxicology screening is described (p. 608).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: no patient admitted to previous cocaine use (p. 608).

comparison.controls: Two comparisons. Within-person: each patient's values after the infusion against the same patient's values after cocaine and at baseline (the comparison the conclusion rests on). Between-arm: the 6 patients given saline after cocaine against the 9 given labetalol, allocated without stated randomization.
comparison.matching: None. No matching, no adjustment, and no test of baseline comparability between arms is reported, although Table I shows the arms differed in heart rate, mean arterial pressure, coronary arterial area and achieved cocaine concentration.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable in the usual sense (no prior cocaine exposure). Unmeasured are the degree of adrenergic blockade achieved by labetalol, each patient's coronary reactivity before cocaine, and how coronary disease severity and sex were distributed between the arms.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The saline arm received the same cocaine dose, premedication and contrast, differing only in the infusion given afterwards.

outcomes.instruments: Systemic arterial pressure through the side-port of a 9F femoral arterial sheath; heart rate by electrocardiographic monitoring; cineangiography of the left coronary artery with computer-assisted quantitative coronary analysis (Cardiovascular Angiography Analysis System, Rotterdam), measuring coronary arterial area in mm2 in a proximal, a middle and a distal left anterior descending segment chosen as free of atherosclerotic narrowing (pp. 608-609).
outcomes.validity_norms: Quantitative angiography of disease-free segments is the standard method of the period and was used identically in the companion propranolol study, which makes the two comparable in technique. The outcome is lumen geometry, not perfusion: unlike the 1990 study, no coronary blood flow, coronary vascular resistance or transcardiac oxygen content difference was measured here, so nothing can be said about the resistance vessels, which is where propranolol's effect was largest.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Alleviation' of vasoconstriction is operationalized as a change in mean coronary arterial area 5 minutes after the infusion relative to the post-cocaine value; no ischemic or clinical endpoint was defined, and no adverse events are reported either way.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Three variables (heart rate, mean arterial pressure, coronary arterial area) at three time points in two arms, by repeated-measures analysis of variance at an uncorrected threshold of p < 0.05 (p. 609).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. The 1990 companion study states that analyses were done without knowledge of the agent given; this paper makes no such statement, and no blinding of patients or operators is described.

analysis.effect_sizes: Means +/- 1 standard deviation, compared within each arm across the three time points by repeated-measures analysis of variance; p < 0.05 significant (p. 609). Table I (p. 609), labetalol arm (n = 9): heart rate 71 +/- 12, 73 +/- 12 and 69 +/- 12 beats/min at baseline, after cocaine and after labetalol, with no value significantly different from baseline; mean arterial pressure 107 +/- 13, 117 +/- 14 (p < 0.05 against baseline) and 110 +/- 11 (not marked as different from baseline); coronary arterial area 3.80 +/- 1.42, 3.47 +/- 1.37 and 3.37 +/- 1.32 mm2, both post-cocaine values significantly below baseline. Saline arm (n = 6): heart rate 83 +/- 14, 83 +/- 15, 84 +/- 15; mean arterial pressure 96 +/- 14, 106 +/- 14 and 102 +/- 10, both raised against baseline; coronary arterial area 4.59 +/- 3.86, 3.82 +/- 3.14 and 3.70 +/- 3.10 mm2, both below baseline. Editors' calculation from these means: coronary area fell 8.7% after cocaine and 11.3% after labetalol relative to baseline in the labetalol arm, and 16.8% and 19.4% in the saline arm; the mean arterial pressure fall after labetalol is 7 mm Hg, about 60% of the 10 mm Hg rise cocaine had produced. No confidence intervals, no effect sizes and no between-arm test are reported anywhere in the paper.
analysis.covariates: None. No adjustment for the baseline differences between arms, for coronary disease severity, for sex or for the different cocaine concentrations achieved.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol, registration or prespecified primary outcome is mentioned. Approved by the Human Subjects Review Committee of the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center with written informed consent (p. 608). Manuscript submitted 15 September 1992 and accepted 16 November 1992 (p. 608).
analysis.selective_reporting: The Results section contains no numbers at all: two short paragraphs state directions of change and refer the reader to Table I and Figure 1. The abstract's quantitative headline (13% +/- 10% decrease in coronary arterial area in 32 of 40 segments) appears nowhere in the body, the table or the figure, and the segment-level analysis behind it is never described. Table I marks only comparisons with baseline, while the abstract's p < 0.05 concerns the post-cocaine to post-labetalol fall in pressure, a comparison whose test is not shown.
analysis.power: Not addressed. With 9 patients in the labetalol arm and 6 in the saline arm, the finding of interest is a null result for coronary area (3.47 to 3.37 mm2); no equivalence margin or confidence interval is given, so the study cannot distinguish 'labetalol does not relieve vasoconstriction' from 'this study was too small to detect relief'.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 9 cocaine-naive catheterization patients, intranasal cocaine narrowed disease-free left anterior descending segments by about 9% and raised mean arterial pressure by 10 mm Hg; intravenous labetalol 0.25 mg/kg then lowered mean arterial pressure by 7 mm Hg while mean coronary arterial area moved from 3.47 to 3.37 mm2, remaining significantly below the pre-cocaine value. In the 6 patients given saline instead, the post-cocaine state persisted unchanged. Heart rate did not change at any point in either arm.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and the closing paragraph conclude that labetalol reverses the cocaine-induced rise in arterial pressure but does not alleviate cocaine-induced coronary vasoconstriction, and the discussion adds that nitroglycerin, shown elsewhere to reverse both, may be preferable in patients with cocaine-associated chest pain (pp. 608, 610). Three gaps. First, a null result in 9 patients with no confidence interval or equivalence margin is reported as an established absence of effect. Second, the explanation offered, that labetalol's beta-blocking activity predominates over its alpha-blocking activity at usual doses (p. 610), is an interpretation rather than a measurement: no index of alpha- or beta-blockade was obtained, and heart rate did not fall, which is the usual sign that beta-blockade took effect. Third, the preference for nitroglycerin rests on a different study in other patients, not on any comparison made here. The authors do state the two main limitations themselves, naming the single dose and the single route of cocaine, and the single labetalol dose (p. 610).

timeline.event: Same laboratory: intracoronary propranolol after intranasal cocaine further reduced coronary blood flow and raised coronary vascular resistance in 10 patients
This study: intravenous labetalol after the same cocaine dose lowered arterial pressure without changing coronary arterial area in 9 patients
American Heart Association scientific statement discusses labetalol for cocaine-associated chest pain and cites this study

replication.where_it_stands: No one has repeated this challenge, in cocaine-naive patients or in people who use cocaine, and no trial has compared labetalol with another agent in cocaine-associated chest pain with clinical outcomes. The evidence on labetalol's coronary effect after cocaine in humans is this single unblinded, non-randomized study of 15 patients.

funding.funder: Not reported: the article carries no grant-support statement, unlike the 1990 companion paper from the same group (p. 608).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the article (the journal did not require one in 1993).
funding.affiliations_note: All five authors were in the Department of Internal Medicine (Cardiovascular Division), University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, and the Cardiac Catheterization Laboratory, Parkland Memorial Hospital, Dallas. Two of them (Hillis, Lange) are authors of the 1990 propranolol study, so the human evidence on beta-blockade after cocaine in the coronary circulation comes from a single group.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized, blinded comparison in people presenting with cocaine-associated chest pain of labetalol against a benzodiazepine, a nitrate or placebo, with ischemic and clinical outcomes and an objective measure of the adrenergic blockade achieved. Within the laboratory paradigm, a study with enough patients to set a confidence interval around the coronary-area change, and a measure of alpha- and beta-blockade, would at least show whether the null result reflects the drug or the sample size.

domains.note: Allocation to saline or labetalol is not described as randomized and the arms differ at baseline in heart rate (83 against 71 beats/min), mean arterial pressure (96 against 107 mm Hg), coronary arterial area (4.59 against 3.80 mm2) and achieved cocaine concentration (0.14 against 0.19 mg/L); nothing is adjusted and no between-arm test is reported. The within-person comparison is less exposed to this, but confounding by time after cocaine remains, and the saline arm is the only control for it.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: All patients were under catheterization for chest pain and all contributed from baseline, so there is no selection on the outcome; but how they were identified, how many were eligible or declined, and how the 6:9 split arose are not reported.
Both the cocaine dose and the infusion given were determined and recorded at the time; serum cocaine concentration confirms the exposure in each arm.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: No blinding of patients, operators or analysts is described, and the 1990 companion study's explicit statement that analyses were done blind to the agent is absent here. Deviations are not reported, but nothing would have concealed which infusion was running.
40 segments are analysed where the stated method implies 45; the missing 5 are unexplained and not attributed to any patient or arm.

Quantitative angiography and intra-arterial pressure are objective measures, but blinding of the image analysis is not stated and the outcome is lumen area in disease-free epicardial segments only, which cannot detect the resistance-vessel effect that was the larger finding in the propranolol study.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: The Results report no numbers; the abstract's only quantitative statement about the cocaine effect (13% +/- 10% in 32 of 40 segments) has no counterpart anywhere in the paper, and the test behind the abstract's p < 0.05 for the fall in pressure after labetalol is not shown in Table I, which marks only comparisons with baseline.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The measurements are objective and the design has the right shape for its question, with a parallel saline arm, but the comparison is unrandomized between groups that differ at baseline, nothing is blinded, and the quantitative results live almost entirely in a single table whose numbers the abstract does not match. The source can be cited for what happened to mean arterial pressure, heart rate and quantitative coronary arterial area in 9 cocaine-naive patients given labetalol 0.25 mg/kg 15 minutes after intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg, and in 6 given saline, as a single small unblinded study. It cannot be cited for the clinical effect of labetalol in people who use cocaine, for a comparison between labetalol and propranolol, or as evidence that labetalol definitely does not relieve coronary vasoconstriction, since the study has no confidence interval around its null result and no measure of the blockade achieved.

key_findings.finding: 15 patients (7 men, 8 women, aged 40 to 79 years) undergoing catheterization for chest pain received intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg, then intravenous saline (n = 6) or labetalol 0.25 mg/kg over 2 minutes (n = 9); none admitted to previous cocaine use.
key_findings.locator: Patients and Methods > Patients, 1st paragraph; Experimental Protocol (continuing p. 609)
key_findings.note: Allocation to the two infusions is not described as randomized and no blinding is mentioned anywhere in the paper.

key_findings.finding: Serum cocaine concentration 15 minutes after dosing was 0.14 +/- 0.05 mg/L in the saline arm and 0.19 +/- 0.11 mg/L in the labetalol arm.

In the labetalol arm (n = 9), coronary arterial area was 3.80 +/- 1.42 mm2 at baseline, 3.47 +/- 1.37 after cocaine and 3.37 +/- 1.32 five minutes after labetalol; both post-cocaine values were significantly below baseline (p < 0.05) and the drug did not restore the lumen.
key_findings.locator: Table I, coronary arterial area rows; Figure 1 (solid triangles)
key_findings.note: Values are mean +/- 1 SD. Editors' calculation: 8.7% below baseline after cocaine and 11.3% after labetalol.

key_findings.finding: Mean arterial pressure in the labetalol arm rose from 107 +/- 13 to 117 +/- 14 mm Hg after cocaine (p < 0.05 against baseline) and fell to 110 +/- 11 after labetalol, a value Table I does not mark as differing from baseline.
key_findings.locator: Table I, mean arterial pressure rows
key_findings.note: The abstract reports the 117 to 110 fall at p < 0.05; that comparison is between two post-drug time points and its test is not shown in the table, whose daggers mark only comparisons with baseline.

key_findings.finding: Heart rate did not change at any time point in either arm (labetalol arm 71 +/- 12, 73 +/- 12, 69 +/- 12 beats/min; saline arm 83 +/- 14, 83 +/- 15, 84 +/- 15), with no value marked as different from baseline.
key_findings.note: Relevant to the authors' explanation that labetalol's beta-blocking activity predominates at usual doses: the usual sign of beta-blockade, a fall in heart rate, did not appear, and no measure of blockade was taken.

key_findings.finding: In the saline arm (n = 6), coronary arterial area fell from 4.59 +/- 3.86 mm2 at baseline to 3.82 +/- 3.14 after cocaine and stayed at 3.70 +/- 3.10 after saline, and mean arterial pressure rose from 96 +/- 14 to 106 +/- 14 and stayed at 102 +/- 10; no variable changed after the saline infusion itself.
key_findings.locator: Table I, saline column; Results > Group I (Saline, n = 6)
key_findings.note: This arm shows the post-cocaine state persists for at least a further 5 minutes without intervention, which is what makes the labetalol arm interpretable.

key_findings.finding: Of the 15 patients, 6 had angiographically normal coronary arteries and 9 had atherosclerotic disease (70% or greater narrowing of a major epicardial vessel): one-vessel in 5, two-vessel in 2 and three-vessel in 2.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (continuing from p. 609 left column)

key_findings.finding: The Results section reports no numerical values: the two group paragraphs give only directions of change and refer to Table I and Figure 1.
key_findings.locator: Results > Group I and Group II paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The authors name two limitations: only one cocaine dose and route (intranasal 2 mg/kg, chosen as one half to two thirds the amount used for intranasal anesthesia, for its established safety) and only one intravenous labetalol dose (0.25 mg/kg, which they identify as the recommended dose and route for severe hypertension), so they cannot comment on larger doses.
key_findings.locator: Comments, limitations paragraph (left column, continuing right column)

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that an agent with both alpha- and beta-blocking activity relieves the rise in systemic arterial pressure caused by cocaine but does not influence cocaine-induced coronary vasoconstriction, and suggest nitroglycerin may be preferable in patients with cocaine-associated chest pain, citing a separate study.
key_findings.note: Recorded as the authors' interpretation and recommendation about hospital care; the study measured pressure, heart rate and lumen area, not clinical outcomes, and made no comparison with nitroglycerin.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's only quantitative statement about the cocaine effect, that of 40 coronary arterial segments analysed cocaine produced a 13% +/- 10% decrease in area in 32, appears nowhere in the Results, Table I or Figure 1, and no segment-level analysis is described in the methods.
reporting_issues.consequence: The most often quoted number in the paper cannot be checked against anything in the body. A claim about how much cocaine narrows coronary arteries should use the per-arm means in Table I, where the fall is 8.7% in one arm and 16.8% in the other (editors' calculation), not the abstract's segment-level figure.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods state that a proximal, a middle and a distal left anterior descending segment were chosen in each patient, which for 15 patients implies 45 segments; the abstract reports 40 analysed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Five segments are missing without explanation, and it is not stated from which patients or arms, so the completeness of the angiographic outcome cannot be assessed.

reporting_issues.issue: Table I marks significance only against baseline, but the abstract's headline comparison (mean arterial pressure 117 after cocaine against 110 after labetalol, p < 0.05) is between two post-drug time points, and the corresponding comparison for coronary arterial area (3.47 against 3.37, reported as not significant) is likewise not shown in the table.
reporting_issues.consequence: The two comparisons the conclusion rests on are asserted in the abstract and absent from the table, so neither the test nor its precision can be checked. The null result for coronary area has no confidence interval, which is what a claim of 'no alleviation' would need.

reporting_issues.issue: The arms differ at baseline on every measured variable (heart rate 83 against 71 beats/min, mean arterial pressure 96 against 107 mm Hg, coronary arterial area 4.59 against 3.80 mm2) and in the cocaine concentration achieved (0.14 against 0.19 mg/L), yet no between-arm test, adjustment or comment appears.
reporting_issues.consequence: The saline arm cannot serve as a quantitative control for the labetalol arm, only as a demonstration that the post-cocaine state persists; any between-arm reading of the data is confounded.

reporting_issues.issue: The eligibility sentence states that no patient received beta-adrenergic blockers for more than 6 months before the study, which can be read either as 'none had taken a beta-blocker within the previous 6 months' or as 'none had taken one for longer than 6 months'.
reporting_issues.consequence: Prior beta-blocker exposure matters for a study of adrenergic blockade, and the criterion as printed does not settle what was excluded.

reporting_issues.issue: No funding or conflict-of-interest statement appears, although the companion study from the same group three years earlier declared NIH and American Heart Association grant support.
reporting_issues.consequence: Funding cannot be recorded as absent, only as not reported.
